video_title: The Bond Market Pain Isn't Over | Weekly Roundup
gist: Veteran fixed-income/STIR trader DCP tells Forward Guidance hosts the bond selloff (10-year at 5.22%, ZB down ~10 points in 2.5 months) won't reverse until the Fed signals hikes are done, AI capex slows, or crack spreads roll over, none of which is happening yet; he frames the real risk as fiscal (a ~$50T deficit), an AI-capex-driven concentration/credit bubble (Oracle bonds already underwater), and a K-shaped economy where diesel and beef prices are crushing Main Street while a handful of mega-caps hold the indices up.

themes.theme: Bond Selloff: Levels and the Reversal Checklist

insights.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.22% and 30-year Treasury futures (ZB) are down almost 10 full points over the prior two and a half months, a sharp reversal from a period when the market had been pricing in rate cuts.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest (fixed income/STIR trader)
insights.so_what: Confirms the bond selloff is severe and rapid, not a slow drift, which raises the odds of forced deleveraging in rate-sensitive credit and equity trades.
insights.quote: just look at where we closed 5.22 on the 10-year... if you take a look at ZB in the last two and a half months, it's down almost 10 full Big Boy points

insights.claim: DCP argues the bond market cannot turn bullish until one of several specific conditions materializes: the Fed explicitly signals hikes are done, AI capex growth slows, refining crack spreads roll over, equity indices show material weakness, or unemployment spikes sharply — and he considers most of these unlikely in the near term.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete checklist of catalysts to monitor before repositioning long duration; absent these, the trend stays higher-yields.

insights.claim: SOFR futures currently price no rate cut until December 2029, and the market has swung from pricing roughly three-quarters of a percentage point of cuts to now pricing about four quarter-point hikes since the war began around March.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: A repricing of this magnitude in months shows how violently rate expectations have reversed, and any dovish surprise from here would be a major catalyst for a snap-back rally in front-end rates.
insights.quote: there is not a cut priced until December of 29... We were pricing three-quarters of cuts in. We took the three-quarters of cuts out. We priced in three quarters of hikes. Now we're pricing in four hikes.

themes.theme: Fiscal Deficit and the Limits of Treasury Intervention

insights.claim: DCP estimates the US will hit roughly a $50 trillion federal deficit by the end of the year, and possibly a trillion dollars higher than that.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Frames the structural, non-cyclical driver of higher long-end yields that no single Fed or Treasury action can offset.
insights.quote: we're going to be at a $50 trillion deficit by the end of the year. I mean, it's pretty much a given at this point in time. It probably is going to be maybe even a trillion dollars higher than that.

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Bessent's bond buyback program (buying $4 billion against a planned $6 billion) is, in DCP's view, too small relative to the scale of new issuance to meaningfully move the bond market.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Investors betting on Treasury buybacks to cap yields may be overestimating their firepower relative to the issuance calendar.
insights.quote: I don't think he has the gunpowder to do it to be perfectly honest with you... every uptick in interest rates is just eating up issuance. So okay, you're going to buy 10 billion, but you're going to do a half a trillion in issuance.

insights.claim: DCP sharply dismissed a viral Grant Cardone tweet proposing rate cuts to zero and buying Bitcoin as a fix for the deficit, warning that such a policy path would instead produce roughly 9% interest rates and crash the S&P 500 futures toward 3,800.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Illustrates why aggressive monetary easing is not a free lunch for the deficit problem and could instead trigger a much larger market/rates dislocation.
insights.quote: Do you want 9% interest rates and a $3,800 or 38 thou or 3,800 ES?

insights.claim: DCP frames the bond selloff as a warning shot pricing in an unsustainable fiscal path regardless of which party wins the midterms, since higher spending is one of the few things Democrats and Republicans currently agree on.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Suggests fiscal-driven upward pressure on yields is structural and election-outcome agnostic, reducing the odds of a political fix for the bond market.
insights.quote: I think it's a warning shot across the bow.

themes.theme: AI Capex, Concentration Risk, and Early Credit Stress

insights.claim: Oracle's bonds are trading roughly 10 basis points wide (underwater), and the company recently invoked a force majeure clause to exit contracts, which DCP flags as an early, concrete sign of stress tied to AI-capex financing.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable credit signal (Oracle bond spreads, force majeure filings) investors can monitor as a leading indicator of AI-financing stress before it shows up in equities.
insights.quote: Oracle's bonds are upside down by at least 10 bips now, right? And they just did a force majeure, which is crazy.

insights.claim: A Goldman Sachs chart cited in the conversation shows more than 50% of S&P 500 constituents now exhibit negative beta to the index itself — an unprecedented level that means the index's moves are being driven by a small handful of mega-cap names moving opposite most of the market.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A hard statistical confirmation of extreme index concentration; a reversal in the mega-cap leaders could see the majority of constituents actually rally, not fall, complicating simple index-level bearish bets.
insights.quote: we've never had this amount of constituents with negative beta to the index itself... over 50% of the constituents of the S&P 500 are now moving with negative beta to the index itself

insights.claim: The equal-weighted S&P 500 (RSP) is down about 6% from its highs even as the cap-weighted index sits near all-time highs, showing headline index strength is being carried almost entirely by the Mag 7/AI mega-caps.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Confirms that broad-market breadth is deteriorating even as the S&P 500 headline looks fine, a classic late-cycle concentration warning sign.
insights.quote: Well, RSP is down. Equal's down 6% from the highs.

insights.claim: A widely circulated list (from Compound 248) shows many well-known, fundamentally sound non-AI companies down 30-98% from their all-time highs — including Nike (-84%), PayPal (-83%), Trade Desk (-98%), Disney (-50%), and McDonald's (-31%) — illustrating that market strength outside AI/Mag7 names is far weaker than the S&P 500 headline suggests.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Reinforces a stock-picking opportunity thesis: quality non-AI names trading at multi-year lows could be attractive once the concentration/rotation trade unwinds.
insights.quote: Nike down 84, McDonald's down 31, CarMax down 63, PayPal down 83, Pepsi down 34, Disney down 50, Dicks down 46

insights.claim: If expressing a bearish equity view, DCP says he would rather short an AI/mega-cap leader outright than short already-beaten-down laggards or small caps (Russell), viewing today's AI enthusiasm as structurally similar to the 2008 subprime crisis and the dot-com bubble in terms of leverage and greed — though he cautions AI 'isn't there yet' since no major AI player has turned a profit.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Suggests the highest-conviction short in this cycle is a specific overvalued AI winner, not the market's already-cheap laggards, as the asymmetric put position.
insights.quote: I would rather have an aggressive short position on something in AI that I think is just wrong... I view AI in the very same vein that I viewed 2008 in the mortgage subprime crisis and the dotcom market.

themes.theme: K-Shaped Economy: Diesel, Beef, and Small-Business Credit

insights.claim: Diesel prices have spiked to roughly $9/gallon in parts of the country and about $7/gallon in Chicago, which DCP says will pass through into food service, retail, trucking, and any wheeled logistics (citing Amazon as an example).
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Rising diesel is a real-economy inflation transmission mechanism largely invisible in headline equity indices, squeezing consumer and logistics margins.
insights.quote: I was just in C.I. Diesel was nine bucks a gallon. It's seven bucks a gallon in Chicago.

insights.claim: DCP says beef costs in his own school catering business have fully doubled compared to two to three years ago, driven by a cattle market he expects will not improve soon.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: A concrete, first-hand data point on food-cost inflation hitting small/mid-size operators well before it shows in official CPI prints.
insights.quote: I'm paying double in my school catering business for beef from three, two years ago... it's full on double.

insights.claim: Small-business borrowing costs have diverged sharply from large-cap financing: an SBA 7(a) working-capital loan (max ~$200,000) now carries a 12-13% interest rate, while larger SBA 504 loans (up to $2-3 million) still price in the mid-6% range — a direct example of a K-shaped credit market.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Shows the cost-of-capital pain is concentrated in small/mid-size borrowers even while large corporates finance cheaply, a leading indicator to watch via small-business bankruptcy data.
insights.quote: It's a 12 to 13% interest rate right now for an SBA note. Now, you can still borrow on the 504. You can still borrow up to two, three million bucks at, you know, in the mid-6%s.

insights.claim: Regional bank stocks (KRE) are sitting right at their 200-day moving average and may have broken below it, a level DCP flags as important because incoming Fed leadership has specifically called out regional lending as a key area of expected stress.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Gives a specific technical/fundamental level (KRE 200-day SMA) to watch as a proxy for regional-lending stress the Fed itself is monitoring.
insights.quote: if you look at KRE on a daily, it literally is sitting on the 200 right now... Worsh has specifically called out lending. So, the stressors that you're going to see are going to manifest in regional lending.

themes.theme: Fed Policy Under Warsh and the Perkins Framework

insights.claim: A recent Federal Reserve board vote under new leadership (Warsh) was unanimous, which DCP called a genuine surprise and a positive sign, since a hawkish or dovish faction breaking away would have made policy execution far messier.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Fed unity reduces near-term policy-surprise risk, but DCP frames it as necessary groundwork rather than evidence the Fed's underlying problem is solved.
insights.quote: I think Worsh has everyone on the same page, which is surprising... a unanimous vote was kind of a surprise to me.

insights.claim: DCP repeatedly cites a framework from macro strategist Dario Perkins: markets shouldn't worry about problems the Fed can fix (liquidity crises), but should worry about problems the Fed can't fix — specifically a runaway deficit or an energy supply shock.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: A mental model for triaging macro risks: rates/liquidity stress is a 'Fed can fix it' problem, but fiscal and energy-supply shocks are not, and deserve more attention from investors right now.
insights.quote: Don't worry about the stuff that the Fed can fix. Worry about the stuff the Fed can't fix.

insights.claim: DCP argues that hiking rates into an oil supply shock (driven by the Iran conflict) is largely ineffective at containing true inflation — it may dampen some consumer-level pass-through but will not fix the underlying oil supply problem.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Implies rate hikes aimed at supply-shock inflation are a blunt, partially futile tool, raising the risk of an overtightening policy mistake.
insights.quote: why are you hiking into a supply shock? It's not going to be effective at containing inflation... it's still not going to fix the oil problem.

insights.claim: DCP warns of a specific policy-mistake scenario: the Fed hikes multiple times (a full percentage point), directly triggering an AI-capex-driven meltdown and leaving 'bag holders everywhere,' explicitly comparing it to the Fed cutting too much in 1998 and then hiking into the dot-com bust.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: A concrete tail-risk scenario worth hedging: Fed tightening colliding with an already-fragile AI-financed rally.
insights.quote: They could hike four times, get you a one point hike right into an AI capex meltdown that blows up all of it and there are bag holders everywhere.

insights.claim: DCP predicts Iran has strong incentive to stall negotiations past the US midterms, betting that a different US administration would be easier to negotiate with, and expects Iran will not meaningfully settle while Trump remains in office.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Suggests investors shouldn't expect a near-term geopolitical resolution that would relieve the oil-driven inflation and yield pressure before the midterms.
insights.quote: If I were Iran, I would not negotiate with the United States... I would not give up my hand until Trump's out of office. I would be holding out for a new president to negotiate with.

insights.claim: DCP characterizes Iran, Russia, and China as effectively an aligned axis working to complicate US strategic bandwidth, with Iran receiving Russian and Chinese munitions, equipment, drones, and intelligence support even as China's public diplomatic tone toward the US stays measured.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Frames the Iran conflict as part of a broader multi-front geopolitical pressure campaign rather than an isolated regional issue, raising the odds of a prolonged energy-supply disruption.
insights.quote: Xi, Putin, and Iran are an axis of power that is working in cohort in conjunction with each other to make life as difficult as possible for Trump.

themes.theme: Trading Playbook: SOFR, MOVE, and Historical Parallels

insights.claim: DCP's tactical setup is to buy SOFR futures in the December 2027 (D7) or December 2028 (D8) tenor around the 94.87 level (pricing in roughly one to 1.2 additional hikes), which he calls close to 'free money' (about 100 bps of potential gain) if the Fed pivots — but he says he does not want to own that position yet, waiting for confirmation that something has broken.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Gives a specific, actionable entry level and instrument (SOFR D7/D8 futures near 94.87) for investors positioning for an eventual dovish Fed pivot, while flagging that the trade isn't ready yet.
insights.quote: there is 100 bips in D8 SEP7 sofur that is just free money if we get there... You could literally put on 400 and make a million bucks.

insights.claim: DCP is watching whether ZB futures hold or break the 103 level, which he says is so low it falls outside the last 20 years of historical price charts, effectively requiring 1970s-era comparisons; a break through 103 raises the odds the 10-year approaches 'par' (roughly 6% yield).
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Provides a precise technical trigger (ZB below 103) that would signal the bond selloff is entering historically unprecedented territory for the modern era.
insights.quote: you can't even find a chart in the last 20 years that's going to show you how to price a level on ZB on the futures contract sub 103.

insights.claim: DCP treats the MOVE index (bond volatility) the same way he treats the VIX relative to its six-month spread: the more it dislocates from trend, the more likely a reversal becomes. MOVE was around 104 at the time of taping versus a March high of 111, and he believes a higher high than 111 would be needed to signal a genuine capitulation bottom in bonds.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: Gives a specific volatility benchmark (MOVE above 111) that would need to be breached before calling a bond-market capitulation low.
insights.quote: I look at move as the same way I look at the VIX VIX six month spread... the more it spikes out of line, the more I think we got a reversal coming.

insights.claim: DCP, who has traded eurodollars and STIR markets since 1983, says SOFR today trades exactly the way eurodollars did historically, including a Fed pattern of cutting too aggressively (as in 1998) and then hiking directly into a bubble's bust (the dot-com crash), which he sees as a live risk today with AI capex playing the role of the late-1990s tech bubble.
insights.speaker: DCP, guest
insights.so_what: A veteran trader's pattern-match suggests today's rate cycle could rhyme with 1998-2000: an over-easing followed by a hiking mistake into a bubble's unwind.
insights.quote: sofur trades exactly the way euro dollars did back in the day. The only thing that's different is settlement... They cut too much and now they got a hike. Well they did that back in 98... and then they hiked into the .com.
